title: What Is a Measurement?
subtitle: Marking one star again and again, and what the marks can tell you
body:
Step 1 of 12 read

One star, marked again and again

A measurement of where a star is begins with a mark on a picture. The frame below is synthetic: a star was put at a position we chose, blurred the way a telescope blurs it, and given a little sky noise. Each cross is one mark, the place a careful person would put the center of the blurred spot.

Because we made the frame, we know where the star really is. A real frame never tells you that. The truth is hidden for now. Five marks are shown, each as its position in pixels (x, y) in the list under the picture, and the ring is their mean.

title: What Is a Measurement?
subtitle: Marking one star again and again, and what the marks can tell you
body:
Step 12 of 12 read

What you worked out

Careful marks of one star differ, because the spot is blurred, and the spread of the marks says how precisely a mark can be made. The mean of the marks is the best estimate they give, and its standard error, the spread over the square root of the number of marks, says how near the truth the mean typically lies. More marks lower it slowly: four times the marks halve it. A blurrier picture raises it. Here the truth was known, so we could see the mean land within one standard error of it. The next investigation asks what a stated "plus or minus" claims, and how to check a claim like that.
